newsitem.title: GERMANY: Psychology holding German economy back - IWD.
newsitem.headline: Psychology holding German economy back - IWD.

text.p: Negative psychological attitudes stemming from confusion over tax reform and high unemployment are holding back the German economy, the IWD economic research institute said on Wednesday.

Annual growth in gross domestic product (GDP) is likely to meet the government's target of 2.5 percent, but Bonn can take little joy in the export-driven expansion, as domestic investment and consumer demand continue to lag, it said.
"Consumers and investors have one thing in common: their reticence is primarily psychological," the institute, one of Germany's six major economic think tanks, said in a regular report.
The back-and-forth over tax reform and anxiety over joblessness account for the bulk of the unease, IWD said.
High unemployment diminishes the actual purchasing power of those who have lost their jobs, but also the willingness of those who still have jobs to consume, it said.

This is more a matter of attitude than reality, however, as real household incomes have risen steadily to 2.005 billion marks in 1997 from 1.871 billion marks in 1991, after adjustment for inflation, it said.
Real income is likely to show another rise of about 1.5 percent this year, similar to the expected rise in consumer spending.
Exports should grow seven percent, after five percent last year, as the mark has weakened to an export-friendly level.

But annual investment remains below the level of 1991, as insecurity over Germany's political and social stability has also made foreign investors turn elsewhere, while domestic corporations suffer from weak profitability.
